tema: Time & Effort Idioms — Racing the Clock

vocabulario.palabra: Rome wasn't built in a day
vocabulario.traduccion: Roma no se hizo en un día

vocabulario.palabra: kill two birds with one stone
vocabulario.traduccion: matar dos pájaros de un tiro

cast_dialogue.linea: Time is the only currency we all spend, heroes. These idioms teach you to talk about racing it, saving it and beating it.
I burned the midnight oil all week, but I finished the exhibition photos in the nick of time!
I woke up at the crack of dawn to prepare the catering. With events, it's now or never.
Don't leave everything to the eleventh hour, Ben. In the long run, that stress will hurt you.
Rome wasn't built in a day, mis héroes. Take your time... but when you work, pull your weight!

inicio.definicion_pragmatica: Time and effort idioms describe speed and dedication: 'burn the midnight oil' (work late), 'in the nick of time' (just before it's too late), 'the eleventh hour' (the last moment), 'kill two birds with one stone' (solve two problems with one action).

Don't wait until the eleventh hour.

She always goes the extra mile.

guion: Sofía: Ben! Did you finish the exhibition photos?
Ben: In the nick of time! I burned the midnight oil all week.
Sofía: I told you not to leave everything to the eleventh hour.
Ben: I know, I know. But time flies when you're editing. And hey — it's now or never.
Sofía: In the long run, this stress will hurt you.
Ben: Maybe. But by finishing today, I killed two birds with one stone: the exhibition and the magazine cover!
Sofía: True! Now call it a day and come to dinner.

reading.texto: Working on the exhibition, Ben learned that time flies. He burned the midnight oil for weeks, working around the clock. Sofía told him not to leave everything to the eleventh hour, but Ben likes pressure — he says it's now or never. In the end he finished in the nick of time. Abuela Carmen laughed: 'Rome wasn't built in a day, but you're killing two birds with one stone.'
